content: Consultation can serve as a valuable tool to collect evidence from stakeholders outside the core working group, including academic experts. With the assistance of the technical working group, the secretariat can draft a document that synthesizes the preselected National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) indicators, translates the results for a non-specialized audience, and addresses existing gaps in Human Resources for Health (HRH) data by proposing improvements. This document would undergo review by the multi-stakeholder working group before being finalized. In the context of a national consultation, the secretariat would invite members of the multi-stakeholder working group to a formal executive meeting aimed at validating and adopting the compilation and interpretation of the NHWA. A final report should be prepared by the secretariat and approved by the multi-stakeholder working group. This report should include recommendations for a sustainable model for NHWA data collection, management, and dissemination to inform policymakers. The multi-stakeholder working group could also develop a series of tailored key messages for decision-makers in various sectors during the dissemination process. The target audience would include international organizations, government ministries, public and private sector providers, academia, and the general public, to support further research on HRH. The use of HRH information collected through the NHWA will yield findings with implications for stakeholders and the general public. A clear and practical communication plan is essential to guide the dissemination of these findings to target groups and relevant bodies, both nationally and internationally, including academia. If necessary, Member States can utilize the NHWA platform hosted by the World Health Organization (WHO) to share national data internationally, enabling regional comparisons. The objective is to disseminate data and documents on the NHWA to raise awareness of HRH issues. The communication team, appointed in an earlier step, should establish a system to monitor the dissemination of messages derived from HRH data. A report on the state of HRH in the country should be produced, including a summary suitable for dissemination to a broad audience. Policy briefs should be prepared specifically for policymakers. The technical team could prepare peer-reviewed publications based on new findings. The multi-stakeholder working group should define the various target audiences based on the key messages, which may have been anticipated and incorporated earlier in the process. The multi-stakeholder working group can disseminate NHWA conclusions to the government and parliamentarians to support actions aimed at improving HRH components across all aspects of the health labor market. These actions may include HRH policies, education and training, social protection, and working conditions. The secretariat should collaborate with the multi-stakeholder working group to finalize a report on the state of HRH in the country, along with a summary for a broad audience. The communication team should assist the multi-stakeholder working group in identifying different media outlets and developing a communication plan. Messages should then be disseminated through these media channels, targeting diverse audiences, ranging from the general public to the medical community and specialized medical journals. The communication team should monitor the dissemination of messages across various domains, gather feedback from different audiences, and prepare a report on how well the messages were received to inform the next round of implementation. The technical working group should prepare publications on any new findings identified during the collection and evaluation of HRH data. Subject to any legal restrictions identified earlier, complete or partial disaggregated data could be released into the public domain through specific platforms for data exchange. The custodian of these data will depend on the data provider. The process of reviewing the work conducted to gather, interpret, and disseminate HRH information as part of the NHWA aims to identify strengths and weaknesses in the processes used and propose improvements to support the progressive and sustainable implementation of HRH data monitoring using the NHWA framework. This review facilitates the transition from the initial launch of the NHWA to its establishment as a regular activity with a dedicated budget. Over time, the multi-stakeholder working group is expected to become more technically proficient, particularly in interpreting results and disseminating findings, which can influence political decisions. While the first round of implementation requires significant effort, subsequent rounds will benefit from a strengthened HRH information system, improved interoperability among systems, and any newly created systems, progressively reducing the required effort. Steps 5–7 encompass the annual gathering, monitoring, dissemination, and improvement of HRH data, as well as the development of new sources and providers. However, the inclusion of additional stakeholders or changes in ministerial support and national governance structures can impact the long-term sustainability of the NHWA. Regular revision and strategic planning, conducted every few years, should update the NHWA process. New members may be included, and governance structures revised accordingly. During these review meetings, members should evaluate the governance structure, approve necessary amendments, confirm or update focal points, and identify new stakeholders to provide data or assume responsibilities at the national level. The secretariat should present conclusions from an overview of successes and failures in the last round of NHWA implementation, along with proposals to improve the framework. The multi-stakeholder working group should recommend a process to ensure continued and sustainable funding. Additional catalytic funds could be mobilized to produce indicators beyond the core indicators gathered during the previous round.
